subject: English
description: Adverbs of manner, time, place, frequency, degree; correct usage

questions.stem: Choose the correct adverb: 'She speaks ___ during meetings.'

options.option_text: Confident, the adjective form
Confidently, the adverb form
Confidence, the noun form
Confiding, the verb-ing form

questions.explanation: Adverbs modify VERBS. 'Speaks (verb) confidently (adverb).' Most adverbs of MANNER end in '-LY' (loud → loudly, quick → quickly). Some don't change: fast (adj+adv), hard, well (good → well). Distractor 1 = adjective ('a confident speaker'). Distractor 3 = noun ('she has confidence').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct: 'He runs ___ in his class.'

options.option_text: Most fast (incorrect form here)
Fastest, the superlative adv form
More faster, redundant double form
Most fastest, very wrong form

questions.explanation: FAST = same form for adjective + adverb. Comparative: faster; Superlative: fastest. 'In his class' = 3+ runners → SUPERLATIVE = fastest. Common error: double comparison ('more faster' or 'most fastest') — never combine the two.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the ADVERB OF FREQUENCY: 'I ___ go to the gym.'

options.option_text: Quickly, an adv of manner
Often (frequency adverb)
There, an adv of place
Yesterday, an adv of time

questions.explanation: Adverbs of FREQUENCY: always, usually, often, frequently, sometimes, occasionally, rarely, seldom, never, hardly ever. Position: usually BEFORE main verb but AFTER 'be' verb. 'I OFTEN go' / 'She is OFTEN late'. Distractor 1 = manner. Distractor 3 = place. Distractor 4 = time (when something happened).
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: Very, an adv of degree
Very much, redundant intensifier
Most very, wrong combination
Many, used for countable plurals

questions.explanation: VERY + adjective/adverb (in present/future/positive sense). 'Very delicious', 'very fast', 'very much'. Use 'VERY MUCH' with verbs (I like it very much) or 'much' alone with comparative (much better). Distractor 4 = quantifier for countable nouns ('many books').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the adverb in: 'The boy ran very quickly.'

options.option_text: Boy, the doer of the action only
Quickly, modifying ran (a verb)
Ran, the main verb of the line
Very, modifying quickly here

questions.explanation: QUICKLY = adverb modifying RAN (verb). VERY also = adverb (degree) modifying 'quickly'. 'Very quickly' = adv phrase. The QUESTION asks for adverb of MANNER (= QUICKLY). 'Very' is also an adverb but modifies an adverb. Multiple adverbs in one sentence = common.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Common error: 'She speaks ___ better English than her brother.' (much/many/very)

options.option_text: Many, used for countables
Much, used with comparatives
Very, an adv of degree only
Much many, redundant pair

questions.explanation: MUCH + comparative ('much better', 'much faster'). VERY + positive adjective ('very good'). VERY × comparative is generally wrong ('very better' incorrect; use 'much better'). Other comparative intensifiers: far, a lot, lots, considerably, rather, much. 'I am MUCH happier now' / 'It's a LOT bigger'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose: 'She arrived ___ after the meeting started.'

options.option_text: Slow, the adjective form
Late, an adv of time
Lately, meaning recently in time
Latest, the superlative form

questions.explanation: LATE = late in time (after expected time). 'She arrived LATE'. LATELY = recently / in recent times ('I haven't seen him lately'). Don't confuse: HARD (with effort) vs HARDLY (almost not); NEAR (close) vs NEARLY (almost); HIGH (in elevation) vs HIGHLY (extremely / much). These '-ly' forms have different meanings, not just adverb-of-adjective.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The children played outside all afternoon', what type of adverb is the word 'outside'?

options.option_text: Adverb of manner, describing how they played
Adverb of place, describing where the action happened
Adverb of time, describing when the action occurred
Adverb of degree, showing the extent of the action

questions.explanation: 'Outside' answers WHERE the children played, making it an adverb of place. The most tempting distractor is C ('adverb of time') because 'all afternoon' appears in the same sentence — but 'all afternoon' is the time adverbial, not 'outside'. Manner adverbs answer 'how' (e.g., happily); degree adverbs answer 'to what extent' (e.g., very).

questions.stem: Choose the correct word to complete the sentence: 'The athlete trained ___ every single morning before the competition.'

options.option_text: diligent, an adjective describing the athlete
diligently, an adverb modifying the verb trained
diligence, a noun that cannot modify a verb
more diligent, a comparative adjective form

questions.explanation: 'Trained' is an action verb and must be modified by an adverb. 'Diligently' correctly answers 'how'. Option A ('diligent') is an adjective that modifies nouns, not verbs — the most common error here. Option C ('diligence') is a noun. Option D ('more diligent') is a comparative adjective, also unable to modify a verb.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences uses 'hardly' correctly as an adverb of near-negation?

options.option_text: He worked hardly for ten hours without any break
The teacher could hardly hear the last-bench students
She pushed the door hardly to open the stuck lock
He ran hardly in the rain to catch the last bus

questions.explanation: 'Hardly' means 'barely / almost not' (near-negation). In B, 'could hardly hear' correctly means 'could barely hear'. In A, C, and D the intended meaning is effort or force, which requires the flat adverb 'hard' (worked hard, pushed hard, ran hard). Substituting 'hardly' for 'hard' is a classic exam trap because both derive from the same adjective.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence where the intensifier 'fairly' is used INCORRECTLY.

options.option_text: The assignment was fairly straightforward to complete
She fairly solved all the problems in the test
The weather turned out fairly pleasant for the picnic
He spoke fairly confidently during the presentation

questions.explanation: 'Fairly' is a degree intensifier that modifies adjectives (fairly straightforward, fairly pleasant) and adverbs (fairly confidently). It cannot directly modify a main action verb like 'solved'. Sentence B is grammatically incorrect. Options A, C, and D all correctly place 'fairly' before an adjective or adverb.

questions.stem: He studied diligently for months; ___, he missed the cut-off by two marks. Which conjunctive adverb best fills the blank?

options.option_text: therefore, which signals a logical expected result
furthermore, which adds supporting detail to a clause
nonetheless, which signals contrast despite prior effort
subsequently, which places the event in time sequence

questions.explanation: 'Nonetheless' is a conjunctive adverb of concession/contrast, correctly capturing the unexpected failure despite hard work. 'Therefore' (A) implies the failure was the logical outcome of studying — a logical inversion that makes the sentence absurd. 'Furthermore' (B) adds information; 'subsequently' (D) only marks time, neither expresses contrast.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly applies subject-auxiliary inversion after a fronted negative adverbial?

options.option_text: Seldom does the committee revise its policy mid-term
Seldom the committee revises its policy mid-term
Seldom the committee does revise its policy mid-term
Seldom did the committee was revising any of its policies

questions.explanation: After a fronted negative adverbial (Seldom, Hardly, Never, Rarely), English requires subject-auxiliary inversion: the auxiliary shifts before the subject. Correct: 'Seldom DOES the committee REVISE'. Option B omits inversion entirely. Option C misplaces the auxiliary — it follows rather than precedes the subject. Option D uses a double auxiliary ('did...was revising'), which is ungrammatical.

questions.stem: Four sentences use an adjective or an adverb after the main verb. Which sentence contains a grammatical error in this choice?

options.option_text: The accused remained completely silent throughout the hearing
The new recruit performed surprisingly well in the field test
The fruit tasted bitterly, so the chef added more sugar to it
The officer responded calmly to the aggressive crowd outside

questions.explanation: 'Tasted' is a linking verb (like feel, smell, appear, seem) and must be followed by a predicate adjective, not an adverb. The correct form is 'tasted bitter', not 'tasted bitterly'. This is a precision trap: candidates who over-apply the rule 'verbs need adverbs' choose 'bitterly' wrongly. Option A correctly uses the adjective 'silent' after the linking verb 'remained'. Option D correctly uses the adverb 'calmly' after the action verb 'responded'.
